claims.text: In equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloys, superconducting critical temperature is governed by atomic-lattice distortion caused by atomic-size mismatch.
Greater atomic-size mismatch produces greater lattice-distortion amplitude.
Greater lattice distortion enhances the electron-phonon coupling constant λ.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling raises Tc in these alloys.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNi is a single-phase FCC alloy with low-to-moderate atomic-size variance.
Replacing Ni with Al, Ti, Cu, or Zn systematically varies atomic radius while overall equiatomic composition and FCC structure can be held constant.
XRD peak broadening and Debye-Waller factors quantify atomic-lattice distortion amplitude.
Increased lattice distortion broadens the phonon density of states toward lower frequencies.
The low-frequency broadening of the phonon density of states raises λ through enhanced phonon scattering.
The proposed increase in λ leads to a higher Tc within the BCS framework.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch will systematically increase lattice distortion, λ, and Tc.
The expected Tc increase is approximately 0.5–1 K above the baseline, from about 1.5 K to as high as about 2.5 K.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNi has atomic-size variance σ of approximately 0.03 Å.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNi exhibits Tc of approximately 1.5 K.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNi has electron-phonon coupling λ of approximately 0.6.
The proposed relationship applies only to equiatomic, nonmagnetic, single-phase FCC HEAs at ambient pressure, below 10 K, and within a 0–10% single-element substitution range.
The hypothesis does not apply when phase separation or magnetic order emerges.
A lack of statistically significant positive correlation between lattice distortion or λ and Tc across the substitution series would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention says overall equiatomic composition is retained while Ni is replaced, but the boundary and experiment specify partial substitution in 0–10% or 10% increments while other elemental concentrations remain fixed. Partial replacement of Ni cannot preserve equal atomic fractions for all constituent elements.
The CoCrFeNi baseline has three elements other than Ni, whereas the experiment says that four other elements are kept constant.

The prediction requires a positive correlation, but the numerical falsification example uses |R| < 0.3. A strong negative correlation would directly oppose the prediction yet would not satisfy this absolute-correlation threshold.
